# Introduction

Football matches are difficult to predict, but information about the teams and the match before kick-off may help explain why some outcomes are more likely than others. Studying these patterns could help club analysts and coaches assess opponents and give sports media a basis for discussing upcoming matches. This project uses the Football Data from Transfermarkt dataset (Cariboo, n.d.) to investigate home wins, draws and away wins across the five major European domestic leagues. We will explore the distribution of match outcomes, examine data quality and assess how candidate predictors relate to results. These findings will guide our data preparation and the choice of classification models for predicting match outcomes.

# Framing & Dataset Selection

Our research question is: “To what extent can pre-match team and match characteristics classify domestic league football outcomes as a home win, draw, or away win?” This is a three-class classification problem, with each observation representing one match. The outcome is determined by comparing the teams’ goals: a home win when the home team scores more, a draw when the scores are equal, and an away win when the away team scores more. We focus on the Premier League, La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 to keep the scope manageable and allow comparisons across leagues. The Football Data from Transfermarkt dataset (Cariboo, n.d.) includes match scores and club identifiers, allowing us to define the outcome and link matches to club information. After filtering, the dataset contains 25,241 matches. One limitation is that club attributes reflect the time of data collection, so they may not accurately describe teams at the time of earlier matches. We will consider this limitation when selecting predictors and check that modelling variables were available before kick-off. This will help keep the analysis relevant to predicting future matches.

# Consider & Gather Data

## Data Source
The dataset used in this analysis is the "Football Data from Transfermarkt" dataset (Cariboo, n.d.), publicly available on Kaggle at https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/davidcariboo/player-scores. It includes match, club and competition data for multiple domestic leagues from 2009 onwards from Transfermarkt.com. Two files were employed in this project: games.csv (match level results) and clubs.csv (club level characteristics). An initial exploration of the competitions.csv file was also performed to validate the competitions, but was not necessary in the final pipeline as the competitions in the games.csv file have a competition_type field to indicate if the game was in a domestic league.

```{r} 
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)

# Load the raw data
games <- read_csv("data/games.csv")
clubs <- read_csv("data/clubs.csv")

# Filter to domestic league matches only
domestic_games <- games %>%
  filter(competition_type == "domestic_league")

# Restrict to the "big five" European leagues for comparability
big5 <- c("GB1", "ES1", "IT1", "FR1", "L1")
domestic_games <- domestic_games %>%
  filter(competition_id %in% big5)

# Create the target variable: match result (home win / draw / away win)
domestic_games <- domestic_games %>%
  mutate(result = case_when(
    home_club_goals > away_club_goals ~ "home_win",
    home_club_goals < away_club_goals ~ "away_win",
    TRUE ~ "draw"
  ))

# Prepare home and away team characteristics
clubs_home <- clubs %>%
  select(club_id, squad_size, average_age, foreigners_number,
         foreigners_percentage, national_team_players, stadium_seats) %>%
  rename_with(~ paste0("home_", .), -club_id)

clubs_away <- clubs %>%
  select(club_id, squad_size, average_age, foreigners_number,
         foreigners_percentage, national_team_players, stadium_seats) %>%
  rename_with(~ paste0("away_", .), -club_id)

# Integrate: join match data with home/away team characteristics
domestic_games_full <- domestic_games %>%
  left_join(clubs_home, by = c("home_club_id" = "club_id")) %>%
  left_join(clubs_away, by = c("away_club_id" = "club_id"))

dim(domestic_games_full)

saveRDS(domestic_games_full, "data/domestic_games_full.rds")

```

## Dataset Justification
The raw data consist of 88,958 matches from all competition types (domestic leagues, domestic cups, international cups and national team competitions). To meet the requirements of answering the research question, the data was first limited to matches with a status of domestic_league (63,382 matches), and further restricted to the "big five" European domestic leagues (Premier League, La Liga, Serie A, Ligue 1, Bundesliga) to ensure comparability of club-level characteristics across teams of similar competitive and financial standing, resulting in a final sample of 25,241 matches. This filtered data has four of the five characteristics:

Large: There are 25,241 observations in the dataset, which is more than the 10,000 observations needed. With over 25,000 observations, standard tidyverse operations and most classification algorithms in R remain computationally feasible on typical hardware without requiring subsampling or distributed computing; however, more computationally intensive models such as SVM with non-linear kernels may require longer training time or hyperparameter tuning on a validation subset to keep runtime manageable.

Messy: There is a serious missing-data problem. The total_market_value field in the club data for all 796 clubs is missing. Once club characteristics are added to the match data, attendance is missing for 6,211 matches (24.6%), club formations are missing for approximately 5,021–5,022 matches (19.9%), foreign player percentage is missing for approximately 3,177–3,178 matches (12.6%), and average squad age is missing for 2,172–2,173 matches (8.6%). The pattern of missingness across variables is shown below.
```{r} 
missing_summary <- domestic_games_full %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing") %>%
  filter(n_missing > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_missing))

ggplot(missing_summary, aes(x = reorder(variable, n_missing), y = n_missing)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Missing Values by Variable (Domestic League Matches)",
       x = "Variable", y = "Number of Missing Values")
```
Multi-class: The three types of the target variable are: match result; home win (11,215 matches, 44.4%), away win (7,692 matches, 30.5%) and draw (6,334 matches, 25.1%). This shows that there is a relatively large class imbalance to be considered in the model evaluation, and it is a well-known phenomenon in football (home advantage). A model that always predicts the majority class (home win) would already achieve 44.4% accuracy without learning anything meaningful, so accuracy alone is not a good measure of performance; instead, one should use other indicators such as macro-averaged F1-score or a confusion matrix, and resampling or class-weighting strategies may need to be employed during model training.

Integrated: Match-level data (games.csv) was linked with club-level data (clubs.csv) using home_club_id and away_club_id which matched to club_id. Two joins were carried out: one for the home team and one for the away team to link the pre-match team characteristics (number of players, mean age, proportion of foreign players, number of national team players and stadium capacity) to each match record.

**Interpretation:** 
Centre (mean / median)
Home and away league positions are centred around 10. Squad sizes are centred around 29 players, while average team age is approximately 25.7 years.

Spread
League position has a standard deviation of about 5.7. Squad size has a standard deviation of about 4.9, with the middle 50% of observations between 26 and 32 players. Large differences in scale
The predictors operate on different numerical scales, particularly league position, squad size and average age. This is important for kNN because it relies on distance calculations, so standardisation should be applied before modelling.

Unusual values


**Interpretation:** 
Potential outliers were identified in squad size and average age, while no clear outliers were observed for league position. Zero squad-size values are implausible and may indicate unavailable information, whereas low average-age values around 22 years may still be valid observations. Therefore, outliers should be investigated rather than removed automatically.

### 8.1 IQR-based potential outlier counts

```{r outlier-counts}
count_iqr_outliers <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]

  q1 <- quantile(x, 0.25)
  q3 <- quantile(x, 0.75)
  iqr <- IQR(x)

  lower <- q1 - 1.5 * iqr
  upper <- q3 + 1.5 * iqr

  sum(x < lower | x > upper)
}

if (length(key_vars) > 0) {
  outlier_summary <- data.frame(
    variable = key_vars,
    potential_outliers = sapply(key_numeric, count_iqr_outliers)
  )

  outlier_summary
}
```

## Bivariate Analysis

```{r}
#| label: member4-setup
#| include: false

library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

d <- as.data.table(readRDS("data/domestic_games_full.rds"))

big5 <- c("GB1", "ES1", "IT1", "FR1", "L1")
m <- d[competition_id %in% big5]

m[, result := factor(result, levels = c("home_win", "draw", "away_win"),
                     labels = c("Home win", "Draw", "Away win"))]
m[, season := as.integer(season)]
m[, league := c(GB1 = "Premier League", ES1 = "La Liga", IT1 = "Serie A",
                FR1 = "Ligue 1", L1 = "Bundesliga")[competition_id]]
m[, round_num := as.integer(gsub("\\D", "", round))]

m[, `:=`(diff_squad_size  = home_squad_size            - away_squad_size,
         diff_avg_age     = home_average_age           - away_average_age,
         diff_foreign_pct = home_foreigners_percentage - away_foreigners_percentage,
         diff_nt_players  = home_national_team_players - away_national_team_players,
         diff_seats       = home_stadium_seats         - away_stadium_seats)]
```

Relationships between predictors and match outcome were examined across the 25,241 top-five-league matches. The club-level attributes (squad size, average age, foreigners, national team players, stadium capacity) are recorded as a single scrape-time snapshot rather than per-season values, so they are interpreted here as measures of club stature rather than team strength at the match date.

```{r}
#| label: fig-target
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Outcome composition by league, home win rate over time, and team-strength differentials by outcome."

by_league <- m[, .N, by = .(league, result)][, pct := 100 * N / sum(N), by = league]
p1 <- ggplot(by_league, aes(reorder(league, -pct), pct, fill = result)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f", pct)),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 2.6, colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2c7fb8", "#969696", "#d95f0e")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% of matches", fill = NULL, title = "Outcome by league") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))

by_season <- m[, .(hw = 100 * mean(result == "Home win")), by = .(league, season)]
p2 <- ggplot(by_season, aes(season, hw, colour = league)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100 * mean(m$result == "Home win"),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Home win rate (%)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Home advantage by season") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))

diff_cols <- c("diff_squad_size", "diff_avg_age", "diff_foreign_pct",
               "diff_nt_players", "diff_seats")
long <- melt(m[, c("result", diff_cols), with = FALSE], id.vars = "result")
p3 <- ggplot(long, aes(result, value, fill = result)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.2, outlier.alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y", nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2c7fb8", "#969696", "#d95f0e"),
                    guide = "none") +         
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Home minus away",
       title = "Team-strength differentials by outcome") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))

((p1 | p2) / p3) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
The proportion of home wins is between 43% and 46%, and the proportion of draws is between 24% and 26%, in the five leagues, the differences in these proportions are very small, and the proportion of away wins is between 29% and 32%, the differences in the proportions being again very small. Cramér's V between league and outcome is 0.021, indicating almost no association. Although there are some differences in terms of playing style and competitive structure between the five leagues, the leagues are not meaningfully different in terms of outcome composition, and league identity is a weak candidate predictor.

Home advantage is not stationary. All five leagues show a pronounced decline around 2020, with the Premier League falling to approximately 37.5% against a period average of 44.5%, coinciding with matches played without spectators — an effect Bryson et al. (2021) identified causally across European leagues. This has a direct modelling consequence: a random train–test split would mix pre- and post-2020 matches, letting the model learn from a regime unavailable at prediction time, so a chronological split is preferred.

The ordering is consistent across the 4 features with differential plots separating most clearly on the diff_nt_players and diff_seats with the home-win medians clearly above the away-win medians, and followed by diff_foreign_pct with the latter feature weakly followed. For diff_avg_age there is no separation, with all three class medians close to zero. Importantly, the interquartile ranges of the three classes overlap significantly on each feature. None of these variables alone have a significant impact on the outcome, which means that classification accuracy is likely to be limited and that this is a problem which needs more elaborate pre-match features or models that can combine multiple weak correlated features.



```{r}
#| label: fig-corr
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Correlation between numeric features, hierarchically ordered. Home-side columns shown; away-side columns are structurally symmetric."

num_cols <- c("home_squad_size", "home_average_age", "home_foreigners_number",
              "home_foreigners_percentage", "home_national_team_players",
              "home_stadium_seats", "attendance", "round_num")

M   <- cor(m[, ..num_cols], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
ord <- hclust(as.dist(1 - abs(M)))$order
M   <- M[ord, ord]

cm <- as.data.table(as.table(M))
setnames(cm, c("v1", "v2", "r"))
cm[, `:=`(v1 = factor(v1, levels = rownames(M)),
          v2 = factor(v2, levels = rownames(M)))]

ggplot(cm, aes(v1, v2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r)), size = 2.2,
            colour = ifelse(abs(cm$r) > 0.6, "white", "grey20")) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "r") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 7) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

There are multiple predictors that are highly redundant. The correlation between foreigners and foreigners percentage is r = 0.92, and between home stadium capacity and attendance is r = 0.85 which means that attendance is strongly influenced by venue size but is not a signal in and of itself. The foreigner, national team player, stadium capacity, and attendance proxies are all correlated at 0.44-0.63, indicating that they are measuring a single latent construct (club stature), not separate dimensions. Matchday number is independent of all other variables (max |r| = 0.02). At this level, collinearity can also lead to problems for Linear Discriminant Analysis, because it relies on a non-singular pooled covariance matrix, and can cause an inflation of variance in the multinomial logistic regression analysis (James et al., 2021); thus one member of each redundant pair should be eliminated during preprocessing.

With n = 25,241, chi-squared tests yield significance for practically all the associations reported, with p < 0.001, and so effect sizes are reported rather than significance tests. A further 266 matches (1.1%) are missing or zero club records due to a club table that failed to join; they are not included in the differential analysis.

# Project Planning

## Preprocessing Plan

Squad-size and average-age zeros will be recoded as NA and imputed (median/mode, with missingness indicators); attendance, the most-missing variable, is retained only if it survives correlation pruning, and 266 failed-join matches are excluded. Given multicollinearity from bivariate EDA (foreigners_number vs. percentage, r = 0.92; stadium_seats vs. attendance, r = 0.85), one variable per redundant pair is dropped for kNN, SVM, LDA and logistic regression, though Random Forest may retain all. Home-minus-away differential features become primary predictors, standardised for kNN/SVM/logistic regression. Because home advantage is non-stationary (2020 dip), the split is chronological by season, with class weighting addressing the 44.4/30.5/25.1 imbalance.

## Model Plan

### Multinomial Logistic Regression

Multinomial logistic regression was selected because the outcome has three unordered categories: home win, draw and away win. It estimates the probability of each outcome and provides an interpretable baseline for comparison with the other models (James et al., 2021). The bivariate EDA showed considerable overlap between the outcome groups, so we will assess whether combining several predictors improves classification. It also identified a strong correlation between foreign player count and foreign player percentage (r = 0.92). We will review redundant predictors to reduce multicollinearity and handle missing values and implausible zeros before fitting the model. Club attributes recorded at the time of data collection will need to be checked for historical availability before being included as pre-match predictors. A limitation of multinomial logistic regression is that it assumes linear relationships between numerical predictors and the log-odds of each outcome relative to a reference category. It may therefore miss more complex patterns unless suitable transformations or interactions are included. Performance will be assessed using a chronological data split and the same evaluation metrics as the other models.

### Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)

LDA was chosen because the outcome of the target variable has three classes, namely home win (44.4%), away win (30.5%) and draw (25.1%) and LDA with a shared covariance structure can naturally be extended to the case of multi classes. Unlike for the distance-based methods like kNN, LDA does not need to standardise the predictors in advance, as it operates by a pooled covariance matrix, and not the raw Euclidean distance. The bivariate EDA showed however that some club-characteristic predictors (e.g. foreigners_number and foreigners_percentage) were highly multicollinear (r = 0.92), which could make the pooled covariance matrix on which LDA depends singular; redundant variables will thus need to be removed or transformed prior to LDA. The univariate EDA also revealed the presence of missing values in some of the important numerical predictors (up to 24.6% in attendance) and unreasonable values of zero for the predictors of the squad size and average age, which can be misleading in the computation of the class means and covariances used by the LDA, and should be imputed or removed in the pre-processing stage. Moreover, there is much overlap between the distributions of the predictors within the three classes, so the classes are not perfectly linearly separable, and LDA is expected to give a good, if not perfect, baseline; the assumption that the predictors are approximately normally distributed within each class and that the predictors have the same covariances within each class should be verified after the final set of predictors is agreed upon (James, Witten, Hastie, & Tibshirani, 2021).

### k-Nearest Neighbours (kNN)

kNN was selected for the five-league analysis because the classification target encompasses three
possible match outcomes, and several key predictors are pre-match
numerical features (such as league standing, squad size, and average
age). This method offers flexibility, requires few assumptions about the
underlying data distribution, and identifies outcomes based on
similarity to past matches; simultaneously, it provides an interpretable
baseline for comparison with other proposed classifiers. Given that kNN
relies on distance calculations, exploratory data analysis (EDA)
indicated the necessity of numerical normalization, handling missing
values, and addressing outliers prior to modeling.

### Support Vector Machine (SVM)

The principle of support vector machines is of maximising margin between classes, which is fundamentally different from the other inductive biases discussed above (probabilistic (LDA), linear (multinomial logistic regression), instance-based (kNN) and ensemble (random forest)), making it a useful point of contrast in the comparison. The main reason for using this method is the ability to fit non-linear decision boundaries without having to expand the features in the original feature space, and this is evident in the bivariate analysis since there is considerable overlap in the features between each of the outcome classes.

There are two practical limitations. At n = 25,241, kernel SVM training scales approximately quadratically with the number of samples (James et al., 2021), making it computationally costly and possibly requiring subsampling or a linear kernel as a fallback. Features must also be standardised, because the kernel is distance-based and the raw predictors vary by orders of magnitude (stadium capacity in the tens of thousands against age in years). Since SVM is natively binary, the three-class problem must be solved using one-versus-one voting, and it provides no class probabilities out of the box, which is problematic if probability estimates are desired for evaluation.

### Random Forest (RF)

Random Forest, an ensemble of trees on bootstrapped samples with randomised features, complements the other models: it assumes no linear relationship between predictors and outcome, and needs no standardisation, unlike kNN/SVM. It also tolerates the multicollinearity found in bivariate EDA (foreigners_number vs. percentage, r = 0.92; stadium_seats vs. attendance, r = 0.85) better than LDA or logistic regression, since splits use one variable at a time. Its variable-importance measures reveal whether weak predictors from EDA become informative combined. Limitations: it cannot handle missing values directly, is less interpretable, needs tuning, and does not correct class imbalance (James et al., 2021).

## Evaluation Plan

Since home_win is the 44.4% majority class, accuracy alone is misleading; we report per-class precision, recall and F1, plus macro-averaged F1 as the primary comparison metric, alongside a confusion matrix to reveal systematic errors (e.g. draw being hardest to separate, per bivariate EDA). Because home advantage is non-stationary (a 2020 dip across leagues), validation uses a chronological train/test split by season rather than random k-fold, which would leak a different regime into training. Rolling-origin cross-validation tunes hyperparameters (k, SVM cost/kernel, Random Forest mtry/ntree) without leakage. All five models are compared on the identical test set, with McNemar's test for significance.

## Timeline, Responsibilities and Backup Plans

Work is organised around the dependency that model justifications rely on completed EDA: Framing, Dataset Justification and both EDA sections are finished several days before the deadline, leaving the final 1–2 days free for compilation, formatting and proofreading rather than last-minute analysis. Days below are relative to the project start; the team should map them onto the actual submission date.

| Phase | Task | Owner(s) | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Framing, research question, motivation, stakeholders | Member 1 | Day 1–2 |
| 1 | Data source, integration script (games.csv + clubs.csv join), dataset justification | Member 2 | Day 1–3 |
| 1 | Univariate EDA, incl. missing-value chart shared early with Member 2 | Member 3 | Day 1–3 |
| 1 | Bivariate EDA and visualisations | Member 4 | Day 2–4 |
| 2 | Preprocessing plan, evaluation plan | Member 5 | Day 4–5 |
| 2 | Model justification paragraphs (own model each), written once EDA is finalised | All members | Day 4–6 |
| 3 | Compile model-justification paragraphs into one Model Plan section | Member 5 | Day 6 |
| 3 | Compile references (APA 7th) and AI Use Statement | Member 1 | Day 6–7 (final 1–2 days) |
| 3 | Final proofread, render/knit check, submission | Member 1 & Member 5 | Day 7 (final 1–2 days) |

**Backup plans.**

- *Data/integration:* if club fields prove unusable (e.g. total_market_value, missing for all clubs) or the join fails for more matches than expected, fall back to the differential features (squad size, age, foreign%, national-team players, seats) as core predictors, since these do not depend on the fields at risk.
- *Multinomial logistic regression / LDA:* if multicollinearity or non-normality remain problematic, fall back to a regularised model (glmnet), and report LDA's assumption violations as a limitation.
- *kNN / SVM:* if runtime is impractical at n = 25,241, fall back to a linear kernel or stratified subsample for tuning, then refit on the full set.
- *Random Forest:* if training time or overfitting is an issue, reduce trees or mtry values searched, or cap tree depth.
- *Schedule risk:* if EDA overruns, model-justification work is compressed, but the final 1–2 days remain reserved as float so Members 1 and 5's wrap-up is not squeezed.
